interviewQuestions.question: Build a modal that's fully keyboard-operable. What does that actually require?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd name four separate requirements before writing code, because each one is a distinct, independently-testable failure mode if it's missing — "make it accessible" as one vague step tends to produce a modal that's accidentally missing one of these.

First, **focus moves into the modal on open** — to its heading or first interactive control — since nothing does this automatically; without it, Tab keeps cycling through whatever was focusable on the page behind the modal, invisible to anyone testing only by sight. Second, **a focus trap** — Tab and Shift+Tab should cycle only among the modal's own focusable elements, wrapping from the last back to the first and vice versa, never escaping to the page behind it. Third, **Escape closes the modal** — a mouse-optional close path that a lot of implementations forget entirely, forcing a keyboard user to tab all the way to a close button. Fourth, **focus returns to the trigger element on close** — leaving focus on `document.body` or a removed element after closing reads as the keyboard "losing" the user's place.

Each of these fails independently and looks identical from a visual QA pass — the modal opens, looks right, and closes, regardless of which of the four pieces is actually missing — which is exactly why I'd verify each one explicitly with a keyboard-only pass rather than trusting that it looking right means it works.

**Testing:** whether you have the complete checklist internalized, or would ship a modal missing one of these four pieces.

interviewQuestions.question: Why does `outline: none` on `:focus`, without any replacement, count as an accessibility regression even if it makes the UI look cleaner?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
It removes the *only* visual signal a keyboard user has for where they currently are on the page. A mouse user always has a visible cursor; a keyboard user's only equivalent is the focus indicator, so removing it doesn't just make things look cleaner — it makes the interface genuinely unusable for keyboard navigation, since there's no way to tell which element would activate on the next Enter press.

The reason this shipped so often in real codebases: `:focus` fires on *every* focus event, including a mouse click landing on a button — which does produce a slightly odd-looking ring that designers reasonably wanted gone. The fix that actually solves the design complaint without breaking keyboard use is `:focus-visible`, which the browser applies based on a heuristic for whether the interaction was keyboard-driven — so `.btn:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid blue; }` shows the ring for Tab navigation and stays invisible for a mouse click, with no `outline: none` needed anywhere.

I'd flag this proactively in a code review the moment I saw a bare `outline: none` with no `:focus-visible` counterpart nearby, since it's one of the most common, easy-to-miss regressions that a purely visual review will never catch.

**Testing:** whether you understand focus indication as a functional requirement, not a stylistic detail that's safe to remove for aesthetics.

interviewQuestions.question: Your team adopted client-side routing for a big performance win, and afterward a usability report says screen reader users can no longer tell when navigation happens. What broke, and how do you fix it?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
A traditional multi-page navigation resets focus to the top of the new document automatically, as a side effect of the browser loading a whole new page — nobody had to write code for that, so nobody noticed it was doing real accessibility work. Client-side routing removes the full navigation entirely and swaps content via JavaScript, which means that automatic reset disappears too, silently, with nothing replacing it unless someone builds it deliberately.

The fix has two parts. First, on every route change, move focus explicitly — typically to the new page's `<h1>`, with `tabindex="-1"` added so a normally non-focusable heading can accept programmatic focus. Second, pair that with an `aria-live="polite"` region that announces something like "Navigated to Settings," so the transition itself is communicated even before the user starts exploring the new heading's content — moving focus alone tells a screen reader user *where* they landed, but the live region is what makes the transition itself audible as a distinct event.

I'd also flag this as a class of bug worth testing for explicitly whenever a team migrates from multi-page to SPA routing, since it's invisible in a visual QA pass — the page clearly changes on screen, so it's easy to assume the experience is complete without ever testing with a screen reader running.

**Testing:** whether you understand what a full page navigation was doing for free, and can identify the corresponding manual fix an SPA needs.
